prime.problem: If each request gets one contiguous KV slot sized for the longest it could become, 60% of the pool is held but empty and only 95 requests fit at 2k. Nobody knows a request's final length, so the memory has to be handed out a little at a time, without scanning the pool and without ever freeing a block twice.
prime.fits: Fourth card of group 3. step() called can_allocate and allocate as black boxes; this card opens them. It builds on the KV cache's 128 KiB per token and sets up the next card's question: what to do when can_allocate says no.
expect: a free list, one block table per request, ref counts
block size, free-list structure, watermark, when to allocate
prime.goal: Compute how many sequences fit under contiguous and paged allocation, trace allocate and free_request on a small pool including a shared block, and justify each design choice (block size, free list, free order, watermark).

attend: Why can no request hold more than one partly empty block?
When request A finishes, why does block 2 go on the free list but block 1 become evictable?
What does a block table let the attention kernel do that a contiguous array did for free?
What goes wrong with 1-token blocks, and what goes wrong with 256-token blocks?
The watermark never blocks a running request. Whom does it block, and why?

must: Fixed-size blocks + a block table per request → a request takes a new block only when its last fills → at most half a block wasted per request on average → 237 sequences at 2k instead of 95 contiguous (2.5×)

Allocation pops the free list, freeing pushes back, can_allocate compares two counts → every per-block operation is O(1) → the scheduler can ask for every request every step without scanning 30,469 blocks
A ref count per block → many block tables can point at one physical block → a shared prefix is stored once and returns to the pool only at ref 0
Allocate on demand → more requests fit → but can_allocate can say no mid-request → the scheduler needs a policy for "out of blocks" (preemption)
elevated: Free tail first → freed cached blocks join the LRU with the prefix's head last → the shared first blocks of a prompt are evicted last
Paged attention gathers from scattered blocks → 20–26% slower attention kernel (2023, OPT on A100) → still up to 22× the request rate end to end, because batch size buys throughput
reference: the exact class code and OrderedDict details
the PagedAttention ablation's best ranges (16–128 on ShareGPT)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw a 12-block pool with two requests sharing their first block: the block tables, the ref counts and the free list. Then write the capacity formula and fill it in for contiguous and paged at 2k.
checklist: blocks of B tokens; a block table maps logical → physical block
a new block only when the last one fills: ≤ 1 partial block per request
free list pop/push and can_allocate are O(1)
ref counts let prefixes be shared; a block returns at ref 0

retrieve.q: Explain where contiguous reservation's 60% waste comes from and why paging removes almost all of it.
answer: a contiguous slot must be sized for max prompt + max output (5,120 tokens) because the final length is unknown
a 2k request leaves 3,072 of those slots empty
paging holds only the real length plus half a block on average (0.4% of the pool)

retrieve.q: Walk through free_request for request A (blocks [0, 1, 2], block 0 shared with B, block 1 a full hashed prompt block, block 2 partial).
answer: walk the table backwards: block 2 → ref 0, no hash → free list
block 1 → ref 0, hashed → evictable, still cached
block 0 → ref 1, because B still reads it: stays
the pool now has 8 free: blocks 6–11 and 2 on the free list, plus block 1 as evictable

retrieve.q: Choose a block size for a server with a 2,048-token shared system prompt and many short requests. What do you gain and lose with 16 vs 256?
answer: 16: 8 tokens wasted per sequence, 128 table entries, fine-grained prefix sharing
256: 128 tokens wasted per sequence (224 vs 237 at 2k), 8 entries, but only full blocks are shared, so up to 255 prefix tokens can't be reused
vLLM's 16 is the usual compromise; the paper found too-small blocks read inefficiently

compare.q: Reserve-to-completion and on-demand allocation can both use paged blocks. What does each give up, and which one needs the next card's preemption machinery?
answer: reserve: blocks for max_new_tokens sit idle until outputs grow into them; never preempts
on demand: packs more requests but can run out mid-request
only on-demand allocation needs preemption and thrashing control

compare.q: Course 4 reads PagedAttention as OS-style virtual memory. Which parts of the analogy hold for this BlockManager, and where does it break?
answer: holds: block = page, block table = page table, free list = free frames, ref counts = shared pages
breaks: there is no disk to page out to by default; running out means preemption and recompute
and the KV kernel, not hardware, does the address translation

predict.q: You switch to 4k contexts but keep block size 16. Before computing: does paging's advantage over contiguous reservation grow or shrink, and roughly to what?
predict.answer: It shrinks. Contiguous reservation still holds 5,120 slots per request but now 4,096 are used, so waste falls to 20%: ⌊487,504 ÷ 5,120⌋ = 95. Paging fits ⌊487,504 ÷ (4,096 + 8)⌋ = 118. The gain drops from 2.5× to about 1.24×: paging helps most when real lengths are far below the reserved maximum.
